e.etymology: An English surname, a variant of Sherman, for a shearman who trimmed the nap of woolen cloth. As a girls' name in mid-century America it sat close to Sharon.
A short form of Martin, from Latin Martinus, derived from Mars, the Roman god of war.
A phonetic spelling of Beulah, Hebrew for married, a name given to the land of Israel in Isaiah 62:4.
A variant of Ardath or Ardith. Ardath comes from Marie Corelli's 1889 novel of that name, titled after a field in the apocryphal book of 2 Esdras.
A blend of Jo with the -retta of Loretta, in use in the 1930s.
An American coinage of the 1970s and 1980s, one of many names built with the -ika and -isha endings, close to Tanika and Tenisha.

A Japanese boys' name whose meaning depends on the kanji; common spellings join masa, correct or righteous, with o, man or husband. In US records it reflects Japanese American families of the 1910s and 1920s.
A surname for someone from Flanders, many of whom settled in medieval England and Scotland as weavers and merchants.
Built from Lu and Berta, or as a feminine form of names such as Hubert and Albert.
An English place name and surname from Old English for mill stream. The Australian city was named in 1837 for the prime minister Lord Melbourne, whose title came from Melbourne in Derbyshire.
A spelling of Cephas, from Aramaic kepha, rock, the name Jesus gave the apostle Simon; Peter is its Greek translation.
A respelling of Gladys, from the Old Welsh name Gwladus, probably based on gwlad, country. Gladys spread through the English-speaking world in the late 19th century.
The French and Italian form of Alcides, a name of Heracles, from Greek alke, strength. In the United States it was used mostly by French-speaking families in Louisiana.
A short form of Beverly, an English place name and surname from Old English beofor, beaver, and a word for stream.
A spelling of Ollie, the pet form of Oliver and Olive, both tied to the olive tree.
An American coinage of the 1970s that puts Ca- in front of the -misha heard in Tamisha and Kamisha.
A pet form of names beginning with Or-, such as Orrin, Orville and Ora.
The feminine form of the Spanish word for good. American girls often received it as part of Buena Vista, good view, a place name made famous by an 1847 battle of the Mexican-American War.
An occupational surname from Anglo-Norman butuiller, the servant in charge of the wine cellar, from the word for bottle. The Butlers became one of the great families of Ireland.
e.note: Reads as the job title of a household servant.

e.etymology: Appeared as a girls' name in the early 1980s alongside Avon's Toccara fragrance, which went on sale in 1981.
The Scots word for a girl or young woman, used as a given name in America in the late 1800s, long before the fictional collie appeared in 1938.

assoc.t: Lassie, the heroic collie of film and television

e.note: Nearly everyone will think of the collie from the Lassie films and TV series.

e.etymology: A phonetic spelling of Sade, short for the Yoruba name Folasade, honor confers a crown. It appeared in the mid-1980s with the hits of the Nigerian-born British singer Sade.

assoc.t: Sade, the singer, whose name is said this way

e.etymology: A spelling of Randolph, from the Germanic elements rand, the rim of a shield, and wulf, wolf. The Normans brought it to England; Randolf is also the modern German spelling.
A 1960s American variant of Deneen, close in sound to Denise and Janine.
An old spelling of the English surname Bird, a nickname for someone small and quick or a name for a bird catcher. The Byrds were a leading family of colonial Virginia.
A clipped spelling of Everett, an English surname from the Germanic name Everard, from eber, wild boar, and hard, brave or hardy.
Often a pet form of Zollicoffer, a name Southern families gave to sons after Confederate general Felix Zollicoffer, who was killed in 1862.
